title: My Work in the Manager's Report
description:
The team lead presented. The analysis Minjun had built through overtime last month — reworded, repackaged, presented to the executives.

Afterward the executive said, "Good work on that analysis, Manager Kim."

The team lead smiled. Didn't look at Minjun.

choices.text: Let it go for now. Start leaving evidence.
choices.result_text:
He stayed quiet. Raising this would make him the problem. He knew that.

Instead he decided: every piece of work gets a date and his name stamped in it from here on. Not twice.

choices.text: Brought it up with the team lead directly.
choices.result_text:
A private conversation in the meeting room. The team lead said, "I know your contribution."

Nothing changed. But next time, caution would be there. That was enough.

Opened a beer when he got home.

He knew this was what companies were like. Knowing it and still feeling bitter meant he'd still expected something.

title: Monday Felt Different
description:
Monday morning subway. Before, it was just tedious. Now it's different.

His body feels heavy. Nothing comes to mind. He knows what he has to do when he gets there — but he doesn't want to. Not mildly doesn't want to. Really doesn't.

Is this burnout?

choices.text: It's a burnout signal. Need to adjust.
choices.result_text:
30-minute lunch walk. Cut the overtime. Small adjustments.

Nothing changed immediately, but recognizing the signal was different. Running until collapse and consciously slowing down are different things.

choices.text: Push through. Can't afford to stop now.
choices.result_text:
He gritted his teeth. Just until this quarter.

He didn't realize that thought had now stretched across three quarters.

title: The Headhunter's Call
description:
Unknown number. "Hello, this is ○○ Executive Search."

15% salary increase. Similar industry. A name-brand company.

"Would you be open to a conversation?"

choices.result_text:
He listened over coffee.

The conditions weren't bad. Not a decision to leave — but knowing the option existed carried its own weight.

He hung up. There's still work to do here.

But after he hung up, he paused. Why am I still here? Choosing to stay when you have options is different from staying without any.

choices.text: "Can you tell me more about the role?" (just gather intel)
choices.result_text:
He asked about the company, the team, the culture.

No plans to move yet — but knowing what he's worth on the open market wasn't a bad thing.

title: His Peer's Salary
description:
At lunch, a colleague let it slip. Their annual salary from the recent review. 12% more than Minjun's.

Same entry year. Same grade. An awkward silence followed.

"Oh, sorry," they said. But the number was already out.

choices.text: Formally request a salary renegotiation with HR.
choices.result_text:
He booked an HR meeting. Prepared market data and a performance summary.

Whatever the outcome — asking and not asking are two completely different ways of becoming who you are.

He said nothing. Didn't want to make it weird.

Instead he decided: results in the second half. Prove it in numbers, not words.

choices.text: Asked honestly. "So what would fair look like for me?"
choices.result_text:
His colleague was caught off guard — but ended up being candid. Which manager to be visible to, which projects actually matter for reviews.

Information gained. Bitter, but useful. Another lesson on how to move inside a company.

title: Solo Lunch
description:
He missed the window when the team headed out.

He sat alone in the corner of the cafeteria with his phone. Stock charts.

He wasn't sure if this was comfortable or just what things had become.

choices.text: Alone is fine. This time is more productive.
choices.result_text:
He spent thirty minutes reading industry news. Better than office gossip.

It wasn't avoidance — it was choosing how to use his time. He decided to see it that way.

Eating alone, he admitted it: a little lonely.

Being alone at work had become habit, not choice. Tomorrow he'd try asking first. "Want to grab lunch?"

title: End-of-Year Review
description:
Year-end review. The team lead looked at the paper and said,

"This year's overall: B+. S-grade might be a stretch... probably something to build toward next year."

B+. Good, but not the best. That phrase.

choices.text: "What would I need to do differently to reach S next year?"
choices.result_text:
The team lead gave specific answers. Presentation skills, stakeholder management, data-driven reports.

He didn't walk out with a B+ — he walked out with a roadmap to S. Same meeting, different outcome.

"Understood." He walked out.

A year's worth of grind. B+. He had a feeling next year would sound the same. Was S even possible here?

choices.text: B+ isn't enough. Time to seriously look at other options.
choices.result_text:
He got home and opened his resume file. Needed updating.

The time here wasn't wasted. He'd treat it as a launchpad for the next jump.
